# Riverside Family Clinic — Patient Policies (MOCK — fictional clinic) ## Appointment cancellations Please give at least 24 hours notice if you need to cancel or reschedule an appointment. Cancellations made with less than 24 hours notice, or missed appointments where the patient does not attend, may incur a 25 dollar late cancellation fee. Fees are waived for documented emergencies. ## Prescription refills Allow 48 hours for routine prescription refill requests. Refills for controlled medications cannot be processed by phone and require an appointment. Request refills through the patient portal or by calling the pharmacy line. ## Medical records requests Patients may request a copy of their medical records in writing or through the patient portal. # Type 2 Diabetes Management Guideline (MOCK — illustrative, not clinical advice) ## Glycaemic targets For most non-pregnant adults, the general HbA1c target is below 7.0%. A less strict target, such as below 8.0%, may be appropriate for older adults or those with limited life expectancy, advanced complications, or a history of severe hypoglycaemia. ## First-line therapy Metformin, combined with lifestyle measures (diet, weight management, and physical activity), is the preferred initial pharmacological treatment for type 2 diabetes unless contraindicated. ## Escalation If the HbA1c target is not met after about 3 months of metformin and lifestyle measures, add a second agent. Options include an SGLT2 inhibitor, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a sulfonylurea, or basal insulin. The choice depends on the patient's cardiovascular and kidney status, weight, and

an SGLT2 inhibitor, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a sulfonylurea, or basal insulin. The choice depends on the patient's cardiovascular and kidney status, weight, and hypoglycaemia risk. SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 agonists are preferred when there is established heart failure or chronic kidney disease. ## Monitoring Check HbA1c every 3 months until it is stable and at target, then every 6 months. Review kidney function at least annually, and more often in patients with reduced eGFR or on medications that affect the kidneys.

# Hypertension Management Guideline (MOCK — illustrative, not clinical advice) ## Blood pressure categories - Normal: systolic below 120 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg. - Elevated: systolic 120 to 129 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg. - Stage 1 hypertension: systolic 130 to 139 mmHg or diastolic 80 to 89 mmHg. - Stage 2 hypertension: systolic 140 mmHg or higher, or diastolic 90 mmHg or higher. ## When to start medication Pharmacological treatment is recommended for stage 2 hypertension, and for stage 1 hypertension when the patient has established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or more. The general office treatment target is below 130/80 mmHg for most adults. ## First-line medications First-line agents are thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics,

The general office treatment target is below 130/80 mmHg for most adults. ## First-line medications First-line agents are thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and calcium channel blockers. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be combined together. For most patients without a compelling indication, any of these four classes is an acceptable starting choice, and many patients eventually require two agents from different classes. ## Lifestyle modification Recommend the DASH dietary pattern, sodium reduction to under 1500 mg per day where feasible, regular aerobic exercise of about 150 minutes per week, weight loss for overweight patients, and limiting alcohol intake. Lifestyle measures alone may be trialled for 3 to 6 months in elevated or low-risk stage 1 patients before adding medication. ##

# Metformin — Medication Information Sheet (MOCK — illustrative only) ## Drug class Biguanide oral antihyperglycaemic. ## Indication First-line pharmacological treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, used alongside diet and exercise. It lowers blood glucose mainly by reducing hepatic glucose production and improving insulin sensitivity. It does not typically cause hypoglycaemia when used on its own. ## Dosing Start at 500 mg once or twice daily with meals to reduce stomach upset. Increase the dose gradually every 1 to 2 weeks as tolerated. The usual maintenance dose is 1500 to 2000 mg per day in divided doses, and the maximum recommended dose is 2550 mg per day. Extended-release formulations may be taken once daily with the evening meal. ## Contraindications and cautions Contraindicated when the estimated glomerular filtration

Extended-release formulations may be taken once daily with the evening meal. ## Contraindications and cautions Contraindicated when the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 because of the risk of lactic acidosis. Use with caution and do not initiate between an eGFR of 30 and 45. Temporarily hold metformin before and for 48 hours after procedures using iodinated contrast dye, and during acute illness involving dehydration. ## Common side effects Gastrointestinal effects are most common: nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort, and a metallic taste. These often improve over time or with the extended-release form.
